item.title: President Lula calls Bolsonaro’s Brazil exit ‘shameful’
item.description:
Nobody is saying they know where Flávio Bolsonaro is. Not the cops, not the courts, and not even his own allies. The son of confined former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro has dropped off the map just two days after losing Sunday’s presidential runoff to leftist Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in an election marked by a suspicious ruling from Lula’s handpicked judge. Explosive reports claim Flávio slipped across the border into Argentina and tried to hop a private jet to America. “Latin American news is reporting that Flavio Bolsonaro has escaped Brazil,” Daniel Di Martino, a Manhattan Institute expert on Latin American affairs, posted on X. “Crossed the border to Argentina and took a private flight to the United States.” The Argentine outlet Infobae reported that the 45-year-old politician crossed into Argentina using his national ID card and was set to fly out of Puerto Iguazú, near the…

item.title: Norway and Finland leaders hold rare call with Putin
item.description:
Frontline near Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine quiet for first time in years ahead of planned evacuation A local ceasefire in a southern Ukrainian city under Russian occupation appeared to be holding on Tuesday, with both sides ceasing drone attacks ahead of an apparent evacuation of about 2,000 trapped and desperate civilians. The temporary truce began at 3am in Russian-controlled Oleshky. The city sits on the Dnipro River and is about 3 miles (5km) from Kherson, a larger city on the opposite bank. Ukrainian troops recaptured Kherson in autumn 2022 . Continue reading...

item.title: Who Said It: Marissa Mayer, or Odysseus?
item.description:
Late last year, Marissa Mayer was struggling with what felt like an impossible task. Her daughter Marielle was turning 10, and Marielle’s teacher wanted three bullet points summarizing what made her special. Mayer—the former chief executive of Yahoo and a pioneer at Google, where she was the first female engineer—likes cracking a hard problem. But she felt overwhelmed by the range and complexity of potential answers. So Mayer asked her personal A.I. assistant, Dazzle. Within a few seconds, Dazzle delivered an answer. “It came back and was like, your daughter is empathetic, creative and an animal lover,” Mayer said. She thought it was perfect. In an attempt to express the blend of bewilderment and despair brought on by this New York Times anecdote , I have concocted a quiz: Which is it—a question the tech industry wants me to ask AI, or something Odysseus asks upon returning to Ithaca…

item.title: How ICE Operates in the Shadows
item.description:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents on March 24, 2026 in New York, New York. —Michael M. Santiago—Getty Images During the presidential election of 1863, at the height of the Civil War, federal troops reportedly descended on polling places in Delaware, Kentucky, Maryland, and Missouri and prevented people they deemed disloyal from voting. This prompted a fierce national debate that culminated in Congress passing an 1865 law barring federal “troops or armed men” from “any place” where an election is being held. The central goal of this law, according to its proponents, was “to prevent the President and his officers from interfering in elections,” which are run by the states. Keeping armed federal officers away from the polls, they argued, was necessary to preserve democracy, even in the midst of civil war. This has been the clear law, and the respected policy of every…

item.title: What local election officials found in Trump’s new claims about California voters
item.description:
In summary The Trump administration is demanding that almost every California county review its claims that noncitizens are registered to vote. Some of the information appears outdated, officials say. Election officials from across California questioned the accuracy of the federal government’s methodology for finding noncitizen voters after the Trump administration threatened them with criminal charges last week. The counties on Friday were given 48 hours to commit to working with federal authorities and to segregate ballots from a list of people federal authorities claimed were likely noncitizens. The letters said the list of names were from the same group of 20,000 people that the Trump administration flagged as noncitizens and then sued California over, demanding that state officials not count those ballots until they verify the voters’ citizenship.
